questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to study in an English-speaking country outside of Europe and chose my university based on its course offerings.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy. UQ prepared online modules and webinars that you can complete before your arrival, which help you find all relevant information.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Before the first week of classes, UQ has an orientation week with intro-sessions specifically for exchange students as well as optional sessions for all new students to UQ, such as campus and library tours, speed-friending, wifi setup and tech-sessions, etc. They also have a market day where you are introduced to all the social clubs at uni, which really helps you settle in and make new friends.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
In general, housing in Brisbane is quite expensive. There are many options for student accommodation such as Scape, Unilodge and StudentOne, but these are still quite expensive and you are often bound to a 6 months lease. Instead, I found a room through
flatmates.com
, and I know many other people who did the same. Having an Australian housemate was really helpful when it came to questions about the city, such as where to shop, nice things to do, and it helped me get to know people outside of university. A downside to using flatmates was that listings often show up last minute, with people looking for flatmates two to three weeks before the move-in date. I managed to find housing about a month before arrival, which was "early".

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I lived closer to the city centre, which meant I had a 30 min commute to uni, but compared to friends who stayed on campus or near campus (such as Toowong), I feel like I explored the city much more. UQ is a bit further out of the city, and friends who lived on campus sometimes struggled to get home after a night out and were always a bit far away from everything. I would recommend neighbourhoods such as Woolloongabba, West End, South Bank, CBD or Spring Hill.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: UQ has a broad course catalogue, which can be a bit overwhelming, but you can filter though the options and search for course codes with certain themes such as DEVB for developmental biology courses. The registration process was quite easy. You had to choose four courses when applying at UQ, but these can easily be changed afterwards.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Student central and the study abroad office is always ready to help.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I had no issues getting the courses I wanted and it seemed that UQ adjusts the courses to accept as many students as possible. One of the courses had 3x as many students as the previous semester, so the course was adjusted with more workshop and lab time slots. In my understanding, you therefore don't really compete for a spot on the course but rather on your preferred timetable, which you put together yourself. Lectures are always recorded, so they are allowed to clash, and workshops and lab-work are offered at different timeslots, so you can piece together a timetable that works for you.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I was a bit stressed about the registration process being quite "late", because I did not want to apply for my visa or buy plane tickets before I was officially enrolled, but everything worked out fine. I would also recommend finding some back-up courses in case you get rejected or want to switch out your courses. In the first two weeks of classes you can add and drop courses, and you can even drop courses until later in the semester. Some people enrolled in five courses to begin with and then dropped one course later on, so you can try out your courses before committing, if you are in doubt.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Generally, the level was easier compared to KU, though there were many assignments throughout the semester which I was not used to. As long as you attended the classes the assignments were not so difficult, however, they often require you to be a bit more creative or work with you scientific communication skills which I found refreshing.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The assignments count towards the overall grade in the course, so my final exams only counted 40-50% of the overall grade. The rest was either assignments, quizzes or lab work. Only some parts of the assessment are "hurdles" required to pass the course, and exams are not always hurdles. We also had more group assignments than I am used to from KU. So compared to KU, the assessments are more spread out throughout the semester instead of focusing on one final exam.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Stem Cells, Development and Developmental Disorders (DEVB2000)
Analysis of Scientific Data (STAT1201)
Microbiology & Immunology (MICR2000) 
Entrepreneurial Mindset and Ideation (TIMS1301)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I really enjoyed Stem Cells, Development and Developmental Disorders (DEVB2000), we got to do IVF on mice which was really cool and I found the course really interesting. I also highly recommend Microbiology & Immunology (MICR2000), the course had really good teachers and was well organized. The assignments were quite interesting and focused a lot on scientific communication. It gave a good and thorough introduction to microbiology, however, it did not go into much depth with immunology.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The Australian government recently made the visa application for students more expensive with a price of 6.814 DKK just for applying for the visa. In addition to this, you will need a mandatory health insurance, which you can add through UQ for 1.747 DKK for the entire stay.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Groceries are generally just as expensive as in Denmark, with meat being a lot cheaper and alcohol being much more expensive.
Public transport in Queensland is only 50 cents per ride, so you can travel all the way to the gold coast or to Noosa/ Sunshine Coast for only 50 cents!
UQ also has many discounts on campus. You can get coffee for 3 AUD at certain time slots, and you can buy cheap left over groceries such as pasta or chickpeas for less than a dollar.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: UQ has over 200 social clubs ranging from sports, hobbies and all kinds of interests.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I was part of QUEST (a club for exchange students) and UQ surfers, both of which plan pub crawls, weekend trips and parties.
I also joined the Marine Society, who planned snorkel trips, and fun day tours and movie nights. Marine Biology students might be the nicest people you will ever meet.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Brisbane is located perfectly for weekend or day trips. Gold Coast, Noosa and Sunshine Coast can all be visited by train, and Moreton Island or Stradbroke Island (Straddie) can be visited on a day trip or on a nice weekend trip. You are guaranteed to spot a wild kangaroo on Straddie - they are everywhere.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy, it was not very different from home and Australians (especially in Brisbane/ Queensland) are very friendly and open.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Clubs are easy ways to get to know local students. You can also just start conversations with your classmates. People are used to having classes with different people all the time, so people are really open and easy to talk to.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Restaurants, cafes and bars close much earlier than what we are used to. Many cafes close by 2pm, restaurants by 9-10pm and bars by 12 and some by 2 at the latest.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Australians are very friendly and easy to talk to. People thank the bus driver after their ride, and sometimes you randomly start talking with the people sitting next to you at a restaurant. You greet your neighbors and talk with strangers in elevators. You say thank you to everyone for everything all the time, and I really enjoyed the generally positive energy towards complete strangers.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) See as much as you can of Australia. It is such a beautiful country
2) Join clubs, go to social events, even if you going alone and don't know anyone. 
3) Meet people in O-week and come to club try-outs. Even of you don't join the club you will meet so many new people.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Most exams are written by hand, so you might want to freshen up your handwriting ;)

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Exploring Australia and meeting so many amazing people

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: It is very far from home and the first weeks might be a bit challenging, but everything will work out. UQ also has so many good ressources, so if you feel stressed, lonely or homesick you can have (I think up to 10) free counseling sessions at student central.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
